newsitem.title: HONG KONG: World Bank lauds HK graft-buster but sees problems.
newsitem.headline: World Bank lauds HK graft-buster but sees problems.

text.p: The World Bank lauded Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) on Wednesday for cleaning up the territory but cautioned that the graft watchdog was not without its problems.
In its annual World Development Report, the World Bank said surveys in Hong Kong carried out between 1977 and 1994 indicate that public perceptions of corruption have fallen significantly.
"Indirect evidence suggests that active corruption has declined as well," the World Bank said in its report.
High levels of corruption in Hong Kong in the 1960s prompted the government to establish the ICAC in 1974.
Targets have included a disgraced government lawyer, a corrupt U.S. consular official jailed over bogus passports and even one of its own, a top ICAC official.
It managed to jail a corrupt Customs officer despite the triad murder of a key witness.
But the fact that the ICAC, which is independent of the police force, reports only to Hong Kong's governor is its main problem, the World Bank report said.

"An anti-corruption commission reporting to an autocratic ruler could be used as an instrument of repression against political opponents, and the ICAC has not been immune to such charges," the World Bank said.
It said the ICAC's broad powers could be abused "in systems less committed to the rule of law".
The World Bank report comes with just six days to go before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years as a British colony.
After the handover, the highest executive authority will be the chief executive rather than the governor, which was the top post under the British colonial system.
The World Bank noted that while oversight committees and an independent judiciary act as a check on the ICAC, scandals occasionally develop.
It suggested the ICAC should have further controls put on its power, such as an agency that would report to the legislature instead of the chief executive.

"A tough, independent anti-corruption agency is a potent tool and represents a credible long-term commitment, but there should also be checks on its ability to be misused for political ends," the World Bank said.
Some sceptics fear the graft-busters may find themselves hobbled after the handover -- particularly if investigations target senior mainland officials.
